title: You Fail Dry Four-Card Logic, Yet Your Brain Catches Free-Riders Instantly
description:
Myth vs. Neural Mechanism — Cosmides & Tooby (1989): Why Humans Flunk Abstract Logic (20%) Yet Catch Free-Riders Instantly (75%)!, grounded in Leda Cosmides (1989) (Cognition). Empirical findings show that remember Peter Wason's 4-Card Logic Trap ('If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other' — Cards E, K, 4, 7)? Fewer than 10–25% of university students turn over E and 7 (P and not-Q) — yet when Griggs & Cox (1982) changed it to 'If a person is drinking beer, they must be over 21', ~75% nailed Beer + 16-Year-Old.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, amygdala, ventromedial prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that skeptics said: 'Nothing special about cheating. People just know American drinking laws from real-world memory!' So in *1989 (Cognition), Leda Cosmides designed a brilliant 100%-unfamiliar test nobody in America had ever experienced: 'If a man eats cassava root, then he must have a tattoo on his face' — Cards: Eats Cassava Root | Eats Molo Nuts | Tattoo | No Tattoo*.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Leda Cosmides (1989). The logic of social exchange: Has natural selection shaped how humans reason? Studies with the Wason selection task. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0277(89)90023-1
- Dan Sperber, Vittorio Girotto (2002). Use or misuse of the selection task? Rejoinder to Fiddick, Cosmides, and Tooby. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0010-0277(02)00125-7
- David Premack (1996). Correction to Premack Review of Barkow, Cosmides, and Tooby. Contemporary Psychology: A Journal of Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1037/005010
